t: What GPU Sag Is and Why Heavy Cards Need Support
title: What GPU Sag Is and Why Heavy Cards Need Support
description: GPU sag is the droop of a heavy graphics card's far end, bending the PCIe slot and stressing the solder joints — modern triple-fan cards can weigh 2 kg and stretch 340 mm, far beyond what the slot was designed to cantilever. Over time sag causes PCIe contact issues, cracked solder, and a visibly tilted card. An anti-sag bracket or support pillar holds the far end level, removing the stress entirely.

demo.program:
card_weight_kg, card_len_mm = 2.0, 340
print(f"Triple-fan card: ~{card_weight_kg} kg cantilevered {card_len_mm} mm off the slot.")
print("Slot designed for: far less. Result: droop, stressed solder, contact issues.")
print("Fix: support the far end level (bracket or pillar). Stress -> zero.")

t: How Sag Damages Slots and Cards Over Time
title: How Sag Damages Slots and Cards Over Time
description: The PCIe slot's plastic and the card's edge connector were designed for short, light cards. A sagging card levers the slot's far end down, flexing the motherboard and working solder joints through thermal cycles — the damage is slow and cumulative. Symptoms appear months later as PCIe link drops, artifacting, or a card that only works when propped. Support prevents the slow damage, not just the ugly tilt.

demo.program:
print("Lever effect: far end down -> slot flex -> motherboard flex -> solder fatigue.")
print("Thermal cycles work the joints for months: damage is slow, cumulative.")
print("Symptoms: PCIe link drops, artifacting, 'works when propped'.")
print("Support prevents damage, not just the visible tilt.")

t: Support Pillar Type: Adjustable Posts Under the Card
title: Support Pillar Type: Adjustable Posts Under the Card
description: Support pillars are small adjustable posts that stand on the PSU shroud or case floor and prop the card's far edge — simple, cheap (8-15 dollars), and compatible with nearly any case. Extend to touch the card's edge or backplate, lock the height, done. The best pillars have a soft top pad (no scratching) and a magnetic or weighted base (no sliding).

demo.program:
print("Pillar: adjustable post, stands on shroud/floor, props far edge.")
print("$8-15, fits nearly any case. Soft top pad + magnetic/weighted base.")
print("Extend to touch, lock height, done. Simplest effective support.")

title: Bracket Type: Frame-Mounted Horizontal Braces
description: Bracket types bolt to the case — to motherboard standoff points, expansion slots, or dedicated mounts — and cradle the card from the side or below. Brands like upHere, EZDIY-FAB, and Lian Li (GB-001) make popular versions, some with RGB. Brackets are more rigid than pillars and look intentional, but need compatible mounting points and cost more (15-40 dollars).

print("upHere / EZDIY-FAB / Lian Li GB-001: popular picks, some RGB.")

t: Vertical GPU Mounts: The Sag-Proof Alternative
title: Vertical GPU Mounts: The Sag-Proof Alternative
description: Vertical mounts relocate the GPU to face the side panel on a PCIe riser cable — gravity then pulls along the card's plane instead of cantilevering it, eliminating sag by geometry. They show off the card's cooler beautifully but need a quality riser (PCIe 4.0/5.0-rated for modern cards), cost 50-100 dollars, and can cost airflow. For sag, it is the elegant overkill.

demo.program:
print("Vertical mount: card faces panel, gravity in-plane -> sag impossible.")
print("Needs: quality PCIe 4.0/5.0 riser (modern cards). $50-100.")
print("Shows off cooler; watch airflow. Elegant overkill for sag.")

t: Measuring Your Sag: The Credit-Card Test
title: Measuring Your Sag: The Credit-Card Test
description: Check sag with a credit card held against the card's top edge: a level card sits flat along the edge; a sagging card shows a growing gap toward the far end. More than 2-3 mm of droop deserves support. Photograph it for the build log — the before/after with a bracket installed is the most satisfying comparison in PC building.

demo.program:
droop_mm = 4
print(f"Credit-card test: gap at far end = {droop_mm} mm")
print("Verdict:", "SUPPORT NEEDED (>2-3mm)" if droop_mm > 3 else "acceptable")
print("Photo before/after: most satisfying comparison in PC building.")

title: Installation: Pillar Placement and Height
description: Place the pillar under the card's far third — near the end but not at the very tip — on a flat solid surface (shroud top or case floor). Extend until the top pad just kisses the card's edge or backplate, then lock: the goal is level, not lifted — jacking the card UP stresses the slot the other way. Verify with the credit-card test after.

demo.program:
print("Position: under far third, on flat solid surface (shroud/floor).")
print("Height: kiss the card, then lock. LEVEL not LIFTED (jacking stresses slot).")
print("Verify: credit-card test after install.")

t: Installation: Bracket Mounting Step by Step
title: Installation: Bracket Mounting Step by Step
description: Bracket install: power down, remove side panel, hold the bracket to find mounting points that put its arm under the card's far edge, bolt it snug (not gorilla-tight — case threads strip), adjust the arm to just touch the card, verify level. If the bracket has RGB, route its cable with the case lighting. Total time: ten minutes, most of it finding the right holes.

demo.program:
steps = ["power down, panel off", "dry-fit: arm under far edge",
         "bolt snug (threads strip!)", "adjust arm to kiss card",
         "verify level", "route RGB with case lighting if present"]
for i, s in enumerate(steps, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {s}")
print("~10 min, mostly finding holes.")

t: Use Case: RTX 40/50-Series and Other Heavyweight Cards
title: Use Case: RTX 40/50-Series and Other Heavyweight Cards
description: Modern flagship cards (RTX 40/50-series, RX 7900 XTX class) are the reason brackets exist: 2+ kg, 330+ mm, triple-slot coolers. For these, support is not optional aesthetics — it is slot insurance. Pair the bracket with a case that has a PSU shroud (pillar footing) or bracket mounts. The heavier the card, the earlier in the build the support goes in: mount it with the card, not months later.

t: Use Case: Shipping and Moving a Built PC
title: Use Case: Shipping and Moving a Built PC
description: Transport is peak sag danger — bumps multiply the card's effective weight. For any move: either remove the GPU and transport it separately (safest), or brace it with the pillar plus expanding foam/instapak around the card. Never ship a built PC with a heavy card unsupported; carriers will find the weakness. The bracket you installed for sag doubles as transport bracing.

demo.program:
print("Transport: bumps multiply effective weight. Options:")
print("  safest: remove GPU, transport separately")
print("  braced: pillar + foam/instapak around card")
print("NEVER ship heavy card unsupported. Bracket doubles as transport brace.")

t: Alternative Supports: Fishing Line, LEGO, and DIY
title: Alternative Supports: Fishing Line, LEGO, and DIY
description: The DIY hall of fame: fishing line from the card's far end to the case top (invisible, effective), a LEGO tower under the edge (custom height, charming), or a 3D-printed pillar sized exactly. These work — fishing line in particular is nearly invisible — but lack the adjustability and polish of purpose-built supports. Fine for personal rigs; clients get real brackets.

t: Bracket vs Pillar vs Vertical Mount: Choosing
title: Bracket vs Pillar vs Vertical Mount: Choosing
description: Pillar: cheapest, universal, slightly visible — the practical default. Bracket: rigid, clean, needs mounts — the aesthetic choice. Vertical mount: sag-proof by geometry, priciest, needs a good riser — the showcase choice. All three solve sag; the choice is budget, looks, and case compatibility. Any of the three beats hoping.

print("vertical : $50-100+, sag-proof geometry, needs riser. SHOWCASE")
print("All solve sag. Choice = budget + looks + compatibility. Any > hoping.")

title: Maintenance: Checking Support Over Time
description: Supports need occasional checks: pillar bases can walk on smooth shrouds (check quarterly, use magnetic bases), bracket bolts loosen with vibration (snug yearly), and any case move means re-verifying level. When upgrading to a heavier card, re-check the support's rating — a pillar fine for a 1.5 kg card may be marginal at 2.2 kg. Support is install-and-verify, not install-and-forget.

demo.program:
print("Quarterly: pillar base walk (magnetic bases help).")
print("Yearly: bracket bolt snug (vibration loosens).")
print("After moves/upgrades: re-verify level + rating vs new card weight.")
print("Install-and-verify, not install-and-forget.")

t: Buying Guide: What to Check Before Buying
title: Buying Guide: What to Check Before Buying
description: Check: your card's weight and length vs the support's rating, case compatibility (shroud flat spot for pillars; mount points for brackets), adjustability range (must reach your card's height), and top-pad material (soft, non-scratch). RGB is optional — it adds cost and a cable. Expect 8-40 dollars; the 5-dollar no-name pillars wobble and walk.

print("RGB: optional (cost + cable). $8-40. $5 no-names wobble and walk.")
print("Measure your card height first: the #1 buying mistake is wrong reach.")

title: The Complete Anti-Sag Discipline
description: The master discipline: measure droop before it matters, support every card over ~1.5 kg or 300 mm, install support with the card (level, not lifted), verify with the credit-card test, brace for transport, re-check quarterly and after moves, and match support rating to the card. Sag is slow damage from a visible cause — the discipline removes the cause on day one.

disc = ["measure droop early", "support 1.5kg+/300mm+ cards", "install WITH card",
        "level not lifted", "credit-card verify", "brace for transport",
        "quarterly + post-move checks", "rating matched to card"]
for i, d in enumerate(disc, 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {d}")
print("Slow damage, visible cause: remove the cause on day one.")
